title: ACLU Sues Hartford Immigration Court Over Withheld Basic Case Records
excerpt: The Connecticut ACLU chapter filed a federal lawsuit this week against the U.S. attorney general and Hartford's chief immigration judge, arguing the public has a First Amendment right to docket numbers, case captions, and in absentia removal orders without waiting months for a FOIA response.
body:
• The Connecticut chapter of the ACLU filed a federal lawsuit on Wednesday against U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche and Hartford chief immigration judge Angela Munson, accusing the court of withholding basic case records.
  • The group asked twice for docket numbers, case captions, and in absentia removal orders covering May through July 2026 — and received no response. It argues the First Amendment guarantees public access without a months-long FOIA process.
  • Data cited in the complaint shows more than 99.8% of Hartford cases decided this year with in absentia rulings ended in removal orders, and more than 79% of all cases through August 1 were decided in absentia.
  • A ruling for the ACLU could set a nationwide precedent for transparency in immigration courts, which decide deportation cases outside the ordinary federal court system.

The American Civil Liberties Union of Connecticut sued federal immigration officials on Wednesday, accusing the Hartford immigration court of withholding “basic immigration court records” that the public has a constitutional right to see.

The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Connecticut, names U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche and Hartford chief immigration judge Angela Munson as defendants. It asks the court to declare that “the Immigration Court is bound by the First Amendment right of public access” and to bar Blanche and Munson from blocking the group’s records requests.

Two requests, no response

According to the complaint, ACLU-CT requested all docket numbers and case captions — the line at the top of a court document identifying the parties — for cases handled from May through July 2026. It also sought every “in absentia” removal order issued during that period, the deportation orders entered when people with pending cases do not show up for court.

The organization says it made the request twice — first in July, again in September — and received no response either time. The complaint argues that such information should be available under the First Amendment and should not require a Freedom of Information Act request, a process that can take the government months and allows officials to withhold records on privacy and other grounds.

“While the public can attend court hearings and see the day’s docket, that is not a practical way for people to access that information and get a broad picture of what’s going on.”

— Dan Barrett, legal director, ACLU of Connecticut

Barrett noted that full names are “not normally provided via FOIA” and are usually denied on privacy grounds. The case captions the lawsuit seeks, he said, would provide information that cannot be assembled from a daily docket — enough to track what is happening inside the courts in close to real time rather than months later.

The numbers behind the fight

The complaint ties the dispute to the court’s stark outcomes: data requested by the Deportation Data Project and cited in the suit shows more than 99.8% of Hartford cases decided this year with in absentia rulings ended in removal orders.

A Connecticut Mirror analysis found that in May alone, respondents in more than 90% of cases closed that month missed their court date. From January 1 through August 1, more than 79% of the court’s cases ended in absentia — the highest rate in at least a decade; the next-highest was 2025, at 41%.

The day before the lawsuit was filed, U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., visited the Hartford court and told reporters he had witnessed “purposeful chaos.” Blumenthal said many respondents failed to appear on Monday, in some cases likely because they had not been given adequate notice, and blamed understaffing and a shrinking roster of judges.

“A system that is running amok and doing injustice, and it is intentional injustice, designed to deport as many people as possible as quickly as the system is able to do it, regardless of the merits of these cases.”

— Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.

The privacy question

Release of the data raises real questions about privacy and safety. Some immigration cases involve asylum seekers fleeing persecution by foreign governments, for whom the publication of a full name could be dangerous. Connecticut officials have already grown wary: late last year, state lawmakers passed a bill barring public agencies, including schools, from sharing an individual’s address, work hours, or agency appointments after federal officials sought state data for programs like food assistance that could be used for immigration enforcement.

Barrett said the ACLU is not seeking a proactively published database, only the right to request and quickly receive the records. Sensitive material, he said, can be sealed case by case, or protected by standing rules like those federal courts already use for minors’ names and birthdates.

Why it matters for immigrants

Immigration courts operate inside the executive branch, not the federal judiciary, and their proceedings carry fewer public-access guarantees than ordinary courts. The Executive Office for Immigration Review does publish case-level datasets — outcome, birth year, nationality, language, relief sought — but strips identifying details.

For immigrant communities, including Indian nationals navigating asylum and removal proceedings in Connecticut, the lawsuit’s outcome could determine how much sunlight reaches a system that decides who is deported. With in absentia rates climbing and removal orders following nearly every missed hearing, transparency advocates argue that public access to the basic paperwork is the only way to audit whether the system is functioning fairly.

What comes next

The Justice Department did not immediately return a request for comment. A win for the ACLU could influence transparency practices in immigration courts nationwide, with Barrett expecting the court to adopt automatic sealing of asylum applicants’ names and other sensitive information.
